questions.q: A refactor changed groupBy's signature to use any, and all eleven runtime tests stayed green. What does this show?
questions.explain: Types are erased before tests run, so no runtime assertion can notice that a return type became Record<string, any[]>. Type-level tests check the second contract.
options: The runtime tests were badly written
A TypeScript function has two contracts, behaviour and types, and runtime tests only check the first

questions.q: A test file contains const kobo: number = "1250000"; and vitest run reports it as passing. Why?
questions.explain: "1250000" * 2 happens to be 2500000 in JavaScript, so the assertion passed. Run tsc --noEmit over the test files as well, in CI.
options: Vitest converts the string to a number
Vitest strips the types and runs the JavaScript without type-checking, like tsx; only tsc reports the error
Type errors in test files are allowed by TypeScript

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: toBe uses Object.is: two different objects are never the same, even with equal contents, while equal primitives are. Unlike ===, Object.is treats NaN as equal to itself, while NaN === NaN is always false.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: toEqual ignores properties whose value is undefined; toStrictEqual counts them. Use the strict form when an explicit undefined would change what you send or store.

questions.q: toMatchObject checks a subset of properties. What does this print?
questions.explain: Objects may have extra properties, but arrays must match element by element, including length. To check "contains this item", use expect(cart.items).toContain("RICE-5KG").
options:
subset of keys passes
shorter array fails

subset of keys passes
shorter array passes

subset of keys fails
shorter array fails

subset of keys fails
shorter array passes

questions.q: A test compares a computed VAT amount in kobo with toBeCloseTo. What is wrong with that?
questions.explain: toBeCloseTo is for measurements with floating-point error. Money kept in integer kobo should be compared with toBe, and code should round deliberately where it divides.
options: Nothing: money should always be compared approximately
Amounts in kobo are whole numbers and must be exact; needing toBeCloseTo means the code produced a fraction of a kobo, which is itself the bug

questions.q: A function has a bug that makes it throw a TypeError. What does this print?
questions.explain: A bare toThrow() accepts any error, including crashes caused by bugs. Assert the class, the message, or both, so the test only passes for the failure you designed.

questions.q: In a test, catch (error) { expect(error.code).toBe("EMPTY_CART"); } does not compile. What is the cleanest fix?
questions.explain: A caught value is unknown (TS18046 if you reach into it). Matchers accept unknown and check the class and properties at runtime, which is exactly what the test should prove. A bare cast asserts nothing.
options: Assert on the error as data: expect(error).toBeInstanceOf(CartError) and expect(error).toMatchObject({ code: "EMPTY_CART" })
Cast with (error as CartError).code and nothing else

questions.q: What is wrong with it("refuses a zero rate", () => { expect(toKobo(5, "GBP", client)).rejects.toThrow("Nonsense"); });?
questions.explain: .rejects and .resolves return promises. Make the test async and await the assertion, as the lesson does.
options: The assertion is not awaited (or returned), so the test function finishes before the promise settles and the result of the check is not part of the test
Async functions cannot be tested with Vitest

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A ...Once value is used first, then the default. mock.calls keeps each call's argument list as an array, so the first entry is [ 'GBP' ].

questions.q: Why does the lesson write vi.fn<RateClient["fetchRate"]>() instead of plain vi.fn()?
questions.explain: A mock is a second implementation of an interface. Typing it from that interface keeps the two in step; an untyped mock can keep testing a service that no longer exists.
options: The type argument gives the mock the real method's parameters and return type, so a fake value of the wrong shape, or a change to the interface, is a compile error in the test
It registers the mock with the dependency container

questions.q: fetchRate now returns { rate, fetchedAt }, but an old test still uses vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(1530). What happens?
questions.explain: vi.fn() without a type argument accepts anything. With vi.fn<RateClient["fetchRate"]>(), the same line is a compile error the moment the interface changes.
options: It compiles; at runtime toKobo reads (1530).rate, gets undefined, and the test fails with a confusing message far from the cause
Vitest converts 1530 to the new shape

questions.q: Why is toKobo(amount, currency, client) easier to test than a toKobo(amount, currency) that creates its own HTTP client inside?
questions.explain: Injected dependencies make the seam explicit. Module mocking (vi.mock) works but couples tests to file paths and import order.
options: Functions with three parameters run faster
The test can pass a typed fake client directly; the other version can only be tested by replacing whole modules or by hitting the real service
TypeScript cannot type-check functions that create objects

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The cause option keeps the original error object, which is what the lesson's test checks with toMatchObject({ cause: outage }). Losing the cause makes production incidents much harder to diagnose.
options:
RateError true connect ETIMEDOUT
true true

Error true connect ETIMEDOUT
true true

RateError true connect ETIMEDOUT
true false

questions.q: What does this table of cases print?
questions.explain: Each part gets the floor, and the first remainder parts get one extra kobo, so the sum always equals the total. A good table includes the awkward rows: a remainder, a total smaller than the number of parts, and an exact split.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The directive only silences the compiler; the line still runs. Here JavaScript's * converts "3" to a number. This is why type-only lines belong in files or functions that never execute.
options: Nothing: the line under @ts-expect-error is skipped

questions.q: What does this print when the file is run?
questions.explain: At runtime expectTypeOf does nothing useful: its methods just return true. All the checking happens in the type checker, which is why these assertions must be compiled by tsc or vitest --typecheck to mean anything.

questions.q: Which assertion fails if a refactor changes a return type from Order[] to any[]?
questions.explain: any[] is assignable to Order[], so "extends" is satisfied. toEqualTypeOf demands the identical type, which any is not; that is why exact checks catch loosened signatures.

questions.q: In expectTypeOf(groupBy<Order, string>).parameter(1), what is groupBy<Order, string>?
questions.explain: Instantiation expressions let you talk about a specific version of a generic function without calling it, which is handy for inspecting its parameters in type tests.
options: A call to groupBy with no arguments
An instantiation expression: the generic function with its type arguments filled in, not called

questions.q: A type test file suddenly reports TS2578, "Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive". What does it mean?
questions.explain: That is the "should not compile" test failing. Find out whether the loosening was intended; if not, the change broke a promise the types used to make.
options: The test file has a syntax error
A line that was supposed to be refused now compiles, so the types have become looser (or the test was wrong)

questions.q: Why should each @ts-expect-error in a type test sit alone above one expression, with a written reason?
questions.explain: If the line fails for a different reason than the one you are testing, the test proves nothing. Keep lines small and the reason explicit, so reviewers can see what is being refused.
options: TypeScript requires a reason after the colon
The directive is satisfied by any error on the next line, so a typo or unrelated error can make the test pass for the wrong reason; one small line per directive keeps the intent checkable
Several directives in a row are ignored
Reasons are printed in the test report

questions.q: What does vitest run --typecheck do with tests/group.test-d.ts?
questions.explain: .test-d.ts is Vitest's convention for type tests. The code is never executed, so declare const orders: Order[] is enough to have a value to test with.
options: Runs it like any other test file
Type-checks it with tsc and reports each test as passed or failed according to the type errors inside it, without running the code
Converts it to JavaScript and runs it in a browser

questions.q: Vitest prints "Breaking changes might not follow SemVer, please pin Vitest's version when using it" for --typecheck. What should a team do?
questions.explain: An experimental feature may change in a minor release. Pinning makes upgrades a visible change in a pull request instead of a surprise in CI. tsc over the same files is a stable fallback.
options: Pin the exact Vitest version in package.json and upgrade deliberately, re-running the type tests
Use ^ ranges so fixes arrive automatically

questions.q: A custom matcher added with expect.extend works at runtime, but expect(2500).toBeWholeKobo() is a compile error (TS2339). What is missing?
questions.explain: expect.extend changes values, not types. Merging a method into Vitest's Matchers interface (with its exact type parameters) teaches the compiler about it, just like the augmentations in the Declaration files lesson.
options: A module augmentation: declare module "vitest" { interface Matchers<R, T> { toBeWholeKobo(): R } }
Nothing; custom matchers cannot be typed

questions.q: What is test.setupFiles in vitest.config.ts used for in the lesson?
questions.explain: Setup files run in each test worker before the tests. Anything that must exist everywhere, such as custom matchers, goes there.
options: Listing which test files to run
Loading tests/setup.ts before every test file, so that expect.extend has registered the custom matcher

questions.q: For a public generic function such as groupBy<T, K>, which combination of tests does the lesson recommend?
questions.explain: The behaviour does not depend on T (it is erased), so a few element types cover it. Inference and refusals are where generic APIs break, and only type tests see them.
options: Runtime tests with many different element types
Runtime tests with a few realistic inputs (including empty), plus type tests for what callers get back, what the callback receives, and what must be refused
Only type tests, because generics are about types
Only runtime tests, because types are erased

questions.q: Which set of CI steps catches all three problems from the lesson: a type error inside a test file, a behaviour bug, and a loosened signature?
questions.explain: Each step sees something the others do not. (If tsc already includes the .test-d.ts files, it runs the type tests too; --typecheck adds names and a combined report.)
options: tsc --noEmit (including tests), vitest run, and the type tests (vitest run --typecheck or tsc over them)

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Queued ...Once results are used in order. After they run out and with no default, a mock returns undefined, even though its type says Promise<number>. Give mocks a default (mockResolvedValue) when a test may call them more often than expected.

questions.q: Write catchError(run) for tests: it calls run, returns whatever it throws (typed unknown), and throws new Error("expected the function to throw") if it returns normally. Then use it to print the name and code of the error subtotal([]) throws, and what happens for a call that does not throw.
questions.explain: Returning the thrown value lets a test assert on it as data. Throwing when nothing was thrown is essential: otherwise a function that stops throwing would silently pass the test.
questions.expected:
CartError EMPTY_CART
expected the function to throw

questions.q: Without Vitest, write a typed fake for RateClient: createFakeClient(rates) returns { client, calls }, where client.fetchRate resolves with the rate for the currency, rejects with Error("no rate for <currency>") if there is none, and every call's currency is pushed onto calls.
questions.explain: Annotating client as RateClient is what makes this fake safe: if the interface changes, the fake stops compiling. A hand-written fake like this is often clearer than a mock when the behaviour is simple.

questions.q: Write throwsA(run, ErrorClass) that returns "pass" when run throws an instance of ErrorClass, "fail: threw <name>" when it throws something else, and "fail: did not throw" otherwise.
questions.explain: This is what toThrow(CartError) does for you: a crash from a bug (TypeError) is reported as a failure instead of being mistaken for the expected error.
questions.expected:
pass
fail: threw TypeError
fail: did not throw

questions.q: Write a tiny table-driven runner: for each row, format the name by replacing $key placeholders with the row's values, run check(row), and print PASS <name> or FAIL <name> (a check fails when it returns false or throws).
questions.explain: This is the idea behind it.each: one named test per row, with the row's values in the name so a failure says which case broke. The row type T flows into the callback, so the destructuring is checked.
questions.expected:
PASS VAT on 100000 kobo is 7500
PASS VAT on 99 kobo is 7
FAIL VAT on -1 kobo is 0

questions.q: Write matchesSubset(actual, expected) for flat objects, in the spirit of toMatchObject: return a list of messages "<key>: expected X, got Y" (using JSON.stringify for values) for every key of expected whose value differs in actual; extra keys in actual are fine.
questions.explain: Checking only the keys a test cares about keeps it from breaking when unrelated fields are added. JSON.stringify(undefined) is undefined (not a string), so the message shows it plainly.

questions.q: Write the logic of the lesson's custom matcher as a plain function: toBeWholeKobo(received) returns { pass, message }, where pass is true for a safe, non-negative integer, and message reads expected <value> to be a whole, non-negative number of kobo (with not before to when it passed, for use with .not).
questions.explain: A matcher receives unknown because tests pass it anything. The message is written for both directions: Vitest shows it when expect(x).toBeWholeKobo() fails (pass false) and when expect(x).not.toBeWholeKobo() fails (pass true).
questions.expected:
true expected 2500 not to be a whole, non-negative number of kobo
false expected 3333.3333333333335 to be a whole, non-negative number of kobo
false expected -100 to be a whole, non-negative number of kobo
false expected 2500 to be a whole, non-negative number of kobo

questions.q: Implement groupBy with the lesson's signature so that it groups the orders by status and keeps their order, and print the ids in each group.
questions.explain: ??= creates each group the first time its key appears. Because the return type is Partial, the caller must use ?.: a status with no orders has no group, and the types say so honestly.

questions.q: Write splitKobo(total, parts) so that the shares are whole kobo, differ by at most one, the first shares get the extra kobo, and the shares always add up to the total. Print the shares and their sum for each case.
questions.explain: The sum check is the invariant worth asserting in every row of a test table: splitting money must never create or lose a kobo, whatever the rounding rule.
